bodyHtml:
QR codes have become a convenient part of everyday life, appearing on restaurant menus, parking meters, advertisements, and payment systems. However, cybercriminals are exploiting this familiar technology to trick unsuspecting users into revealing sensitive information.


What Is QR Code Phishing?

QR code phishing, also known as quishing, is a cyberattack that uses QR codes to redirect victims to malicious websites.

Unlike traditional phishing, which often relies on suspicious email links, quishing hides the destination URL inside a scannable image.


How Does it Work? 

The attackers generate or disseminate QR codes that have links to fraudulent websites. When people scan the QR codes and visit the fraudulent sites, they are likely to be faced with login pages, payment pages, or malware installation requests.

Scanning a QR code by itself does not put a person’s device at any risk of being compromised. The risk factor increases when people visit fraudulent sites or download malware.


Real-World Threats

In September 2026, the Federal Trade Commission warned consumers about fraudulent QR codes placed over legitimate parking-payment codes.


Separately, the FBI reported in January 2026 that North Korean Kimsuky threat actors had used QR codes in targeted phishing campaigns.


These examples demonstrate how the same technique can be used for both everyday financial fraud and more sophisticated cyber operations.


How Can You Protect Yourself?

  • Preview website addresses before opening QR code links.

  • Watch for QR code stickers placed over existing signs.

  • Avoid scanning QR codes in unexpected messages requesting urgent action.

  • Access sensitive accounts through official websites or trusted applications.

  • Keep your device updated and use multifactor authentication.

  • If you entered credentials into a suspicious website, change the affected passwords promptly.


Takeaways 

QR codes are not inherently dangerous. The real threat comes from malicious destinations and the social engineering techniques used to persuade individuals to trust them.

By verifying unfamiliar QR codes and remaining cautious about unexpected requests, users can significantly reduce their exposure to these scams.

title: The Quantum Era: Balancing Next Generation Cyber Threats
author: Jacob Weingardt
body: The Quantum Inflection Point: From Cryptographic Disruption to Scientific RevolutionRecent developments, across quantum hardware, soft ware optimization and open source infrastructure, have kinda moved quantum computing from an experimental curiosity into a fast-maturing technological reality. Like, artificial intelligence is now helping drive circuit compression on supercomputers and at the same time room-temperature synthetic diamond processors run in standard server racks, which is… honestly, a big deal. The barriers to entry are eroding, even if people still treat it like a novelty in conversation. And when you combine extreme computational speedups with the rollout of open-source quantum operating systems, the timeline toward practical quantum advantage has sped up a lot, and really, quite abruptly.The Cryptographic Reckoning: How Quantum Threats Target EncryptionThe security of modern digital infrastructure relies on two distinct classes of cryptography known as asymmetric and symmetric encryption. The rapid scaling and compression of quantum circuits impact both, but in fundamentally different ways.The Asymmetric CollapsePublic-key algorithms like RSA and Elliptic Curve Cryptography they help guard digital signatures , web traffic handshakes, and also authentication tokens. The whole thing leans on math problems that classical computers just can’t crack in any quick way, think prime integer factorization, and related number puzzles. Shor’s algorithm does solve them in polynomial time, which sounds neat, but it’s also kind of the problem. If someone gets a sufficiently powerful fault-tolerant quantum computer, and it actually runs Shor’s algorithm properly, then those keys can be compromised in hours, or even minutes. After that, the usual asymmetric key exchanges become completely untrustworthy, like, practically insecure.The Symmetric LandscapeSymmetric ciphers like the Advanced Encryption Standard protect data at rest and bulk network traffic. Quantum computers do not achieve an exponential speedup against these algorithms. Instead, Grover’s algorithm provides a quadratic speedup for unstructured database searches. A 128-bit key is reduced to an effective security level of 64 quantum operations, making it vulnerable in the post-quantum era. However, a 256-bit key is reduced to 128 effective operations, which remains computationally infeasible, meaning AES-256 remains secure against quantum brute-force attacks.Threat Actors and Portable Attack HardwareThe appearance of compressed, rack mountable quantum machines creates kind of separate attack pathways for advanced persistent threats, and more organized cybercrime groups. Right now, threat actors are doing these harvest now decrypt later style campaigns. They intercept and hoard huge streams of encrypted government messages, proprietary designs, and personal dossiers. Even if they cannot make sense of the ciphertext today, they plan to unlock it later retroactively once cryptanalytically relevant quantum computers finally come online.For a long time, quantum computing was basically gatekept by multimillion dollar dilution refrigerators, cooling superconducting chips down near absolute zero. But lately, hardware choices are shifting this whole idea. Nitrogen vacancy diamond centers that operate at room temperature, without cryogens, allow setups that actually sit in ordinary server racks, and draw power from the grid. Also, miniaturized quantum coprocessors can now be pushed into mobile intelligence units, on marine vessels, or into private data centers without any special cooling infrastructure. On top of that, AI services that shorten quantum gate depth let attackers carry out complicated cryptanalytic workloads on smaller, noisier hardware years earlier than earlier theory suggested in the first place.Risks Facing Everyday PC UsersQuantum computing progress isn’t only a thing for big enterprise datacenters. It filters right into the daily threat model of normal consumer devices. Like, a man in the middle attacker with quantum ability might be able to forge certificate authority signatures. They could impersonate banking portals, then silently decrypt web sessions , without anyone noticing.And it’s not just “web browsing” either. Password managers plus encrypted backups are on the radar too. If a vault is encrypted with a master key that comes from older key exchange methods, or uses weak symmetric blocks, then the whole thing starts looking brittle, in a way that’s easier to attack. With cryptocurrencies that lean on standard elliptic curve public key cryptography , transaction signatures can end up more exposed to public ledger extraction, especially after a public key is shown when you spend.Even operating systems aren’t completely safe by default. They lean on public key signatures to validate updates and driver installations. If the signing key gets compromised , then a malicious party could push signed malware straight into consumer kernels.The Defense Playbook: Post-Quantum CryptographyMitigating the quantum threat really means doing proactive upgrades, before universal quantum advantage is reached, sort of earlier rather than later. The National Institute of Standards and Technology has finalized primary post-quantum cryptographic standards based on mathematical problems that should resist both classical and quantum attacks . Among them are module-lattice-based key encapsulation mechanisms, used to establish shared secret keys, and lattice-based algorithms for digital signatures. Organizations also need to enforce AES-256 , and deprecate older standards everywhere it matters like storage encryption and virtual private networks. If you adopt hybrid key exchanges that combine classical algorithms with the new post-quantum standards, it can help keep legacy compliance while still defending against data harvesting attacks . Meanwhile, building crypto agility—by separating cryptographic implementations from application logic—keeps things flexible, because algorithms can then be swapped out more easily in the future.The Constructive Frontier: Quantum as a Force for GoodSo, quantum mechanics kind of scrambles the usual security playbook, but at the same time it also opens really revolutionary paths across cybersecurity, medicine, materials engineering, and that broader fundamental science area. For example, Quantum Key Distribution sends cryptographic keys using photons one by one, and not just in some abstract way, in a very literal way. If someone tries to eavesdrop the key, the act of watching disturbs the quantum state , which then becomes visible immediately to both parties , and the whole thing gets treated as invalid right away. After that, Quantum Random Number Generation leans on genuine physical entropy , so instead of pseudo randomness from software it gives you truly non deterministic randomness. In healthcare, when people simulate molecular interactions on classical computers, the workload grows basically exponentially as you add more electrons . With quantum computers you can simulate molecular docking and conformational changes inside large protein structures, which can shave off a lot from the drug design timeline. And when you can model catalytic centers with enough precision, you can design synthetic room temperature nitrogen fixation routes for fertilizers, which in turn reduces dependence on fossil energy for agriculture. In materials science, there’s also modeling of electron transfer, and that can help in creating high density fireproof batteries for electric transit and grid storage. Looking into correlated electron systems then supports attempts at zero loss power transmission materials that still work in everyday ambient conditions. Plus quantum computing can speed up solutions for messy mathematical optimization, which feeds into better routing, supply chain distribution, and even financial portfolio risk modeling. And not only that, processing non linear fluid dynamics and atmospheric chemistry improves the accuracy of climate forecasts, while also helping identify more effective geo engineering interventions .

title: The Strategic Imperative of SOC 2 Compliance for SaaS Companies
author: Jacob Weingardt
body: Understanding the SOC 2 FrameworkSOC 2 was developed by the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants. It’s this rigorous compliance framework, mainly targeted at technology companies that store customer data in the cloud. It checks how a company handles its internal controls around five Trust Service Principles, kind of like security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, and privacy. Security itself is basically required for the audit, though organizations can still pick and mix which ever of the other principles they want to include, depending on their business model, and what customers actually need. When a company lines up with these principles, it’s basically showing that their systems are well engineered to safeguard sensitive information, and keep running in a way that is continuous, reliable, and not just theoretical.Navigating Type I and Type II ReportsWhen pursuing compliance, organizations have to pick between two distinct levels of assessment often referred to as Type I and Type II reports. A Type I report, it really focuses on the design of a company’s internal controls at one precise point in time, so it can be a strong starting line for organizations that are just beginning their compliance journey. On the other hand, a Type II report is a more thorough check, it watches how well those controls actually operate over a longer stretch, usually about three to twelve months. And since a Type II report demonstrates that security systems keep working reliably as time goes on, without slipping or lapsing, it ends up being the expectation that enterprise customers treat as the baseline during procurement.Unlocking Business Growth and Competitive AdvantageWhile SOC 2 is kinda technically a voluntary framework , in the modern software market it is treated like a hard requirement for doing business. Enterprise customers and their corporate procurement groups routinely want to see a successful SOC 2 attestation first, before they are even open to signing anything or moving their data. Once a provider has that compliance in place, it sort of separates them from other competitors who havent put in the work yet, which removes a lot of friction in the sales cycle, and helps deals close much faster. In the end, a clean audit report becomes a strong trust signal, it reassures prospects and it also helps drive long term revenue growth.Mitigating Catastrophic Security RisksBesides speeding up sales, the meticulous prep work that you need for SOC 2 compliance, kinda reshapes and strengthens how an organization protects itself from the inside. When firms put in place tight access controls, plus ongoing surveillance, along with broad employee training, the chances of a nasty data breach, or ransomware incident, drop significantly. And that kind of proactive security stance helps stop the huge financial pain tied to regulatory penalties and all the recovery work after an event. On top of that, it shields the business from the serious reputational hit that usually shows up once a security failure goes public, and it keeps day to day operations stable for the long haul.Streamlining the Journey Through AutomationHistorically, getting ready for an audit was this super manual and honestly kind of dreaded process, with endless spreadsheets, dull evidence gathering, and real drains on employee productivity. Now, though, new compliance automation platforms sort of flipped the whole thing around, because they centralize the workflows and automatically grab auditor-approved evidence in real time. These smart tools keep an eye on a company’s security posture all the time, and they push out immediate alerts the moment something is off, or when non compliance is spotted, so you don’t have to do the usual manual tracking. And if you pair the automation software with the direction from a trusted compliance advisor, the organization can reduce preparation time in a big way, cut down the human missteps, and also bring audit costs way down.

Security itself is basically required for the audit, though organizations can still pick and mix which ever of the other principles they want to include, depending on their business model, and what customers actually need. When a company lines up with these principles, it’s basically showing that their systems are well engineered to safeguard sensitive information, and keep running in a way that is continuous, reliable, and not just theoretical.

Navigating Type I and Type II Reports


When pursuing compliance, organizations have to pick between two distinct levels of assessment often referred to as Type I and Type II reports. A Type I report, it really focuses on the design of a company’s internal controls at one precise point in time, so it can be a strong starting line for organizations that are just beginning their compliance journey. On the other hand, a Type II report is a more thorough check, it watches how well those controls actually operate over a longer stretch, usually about three to twelve months. And since a Type II report demonstrates that security systems keep working reliably as time goes on, without slipping or lapsing, it ends up being the expectation that enterprise customers treat as the baseline during procurement.

Unlocking Business Growth and Competitive Advantage


While SOC 2 is kinda technically a voluntary framework , in the modern software market it is treated like a hard requirement for doing business. Enterprise customers and their corporate procurement groups routinely want to see a successful SOC 2 attestation first, before they are even open to signing anything or moving their data. Once a provider has that compliance in place, it sort of separates them from other competitors who havent put in the work yet, which removes a lot of friction in the sales cycle, and helps deals close much faster. In the end, a clean audit report becomes a strong trust signal, it reassures prospects and it also helps drive long term revenue growth.

Mitigating Catastrophic Security Risks


Besides speeding up sales, the meticulous prep work that you need for SOC 2 compliance, kinda reshapes and strengthens how an organization protects itself from the inside. When firms put in place tight access controls, plus ongoing surveillance, along with broad employee training, the chances of a nasty data breach, or ransomware incident, drop significantly. And that kind of proactive security stance helps stop the huge financial pain tied to regulatory penalties and all the recovery work after an event. On top of that, it shields the business from the serious reputational hit that usually shows up once a security failure goes public, and it keeps day to day operations stable for the long haul.

Streamlining the Journey Through Automation


Historically, getting ready for an audit was this super manual and honestly kind of dreaded process, with endless spreadsheets, dull evidence gathering, and real drains on employee productivity. Now, though, new compliance automation platforms sort of flipped the whole thing around, because they centralize the workflows and automatically grab auditor-approved evidence in real time. These smart tools keep an eye on a company’s security posture all the time, and they push out immediate alerts the moment something is off, or when non compliance is spotted, so you don’t have to do the usual manual tracking. And if you pair the automation software with the direction from a trusted compliance advisor, the organization can reduce preparation time in a big way, cut down the human missteps, and also bring audit costs way down.

title: Taming Flipper Zero: Preventing BadUSB Attacks
author: Jacob Weingardt
body: Understanding Flipper Zero’s BadUSB RiskFlipper Zero’s BadUSB mode turns the device into this sort of scripted keyboard, so it can spit out commands on an unlocked computer at machine speed, but really it still only works with the capability of whatever account is already sitting logged in , and also whatever the operating system lets that “keyboard” do. So the real danger is not this special Flipper-only weakness or anything like that, it’s more like a messy combo of physical access, casual user habits, and accounts that are way too powerful. If you set up your environment so most users have limited rights, endpoints don’t blindly trust any new USB device, and people don’t leave sessions unlocked and hanging around in plain sight , then you pretty strongly reduce what a BadUSB payload can actually pull off.Least‑Privilege Roles in Azure and EntraIn Azure/Entra environments, start with the identity and roles part a little bit, like don’t just jump to resources right away. Follow Microsoft’s least‑privilege guidance by minimizing Global Administrators, and delegating the day‑to‑day chores to more scoped roles—things like User Administrator, Security Administrator, and Conditional Access Administrator, instead of giving everyone broad tenant control. Then add Privileged Identity Management too, because high‑privilege roles should basically be “just‑in‑time” and time‑bound, so you reduce the time window where an hijacked interactive session could still perform tenant‑wide changes.Also, use strong MFA plus conditional access rules, for example requiring compliant devices and blocking risky sign‑ins. The intent here is that a BadUSB payload, even if it manages to harvest a password, still struggles to get in or to mess with cloud consoles. So the goal is, if a Flipper‑driven script runs inside a user’s session, that user ends up not having the rights to create new admins, register malicious apps, or weaken the security baseline policies in the first place.Start writing a new paragraph here.Locking Down USB Ports on Corporate EndpointsOn the endpoint side, assume every open USB port is kind of a possible entry thing, and wrap it in policy… use Intune device restrictions or settings catalog stuff to deny removable storage access on systems that don’t, or don’t really need USB drives. And for extra coverage, use Defender for Endpoint device control, to tightly manage what devices are allowed to be read from, or written to. You can enforce allow‑lists using hardware attributes like Vendor ID, Device ID, so only the corporate approved keyboards , mice, and storage gear actually work, while anything that tries to look like an extra keyboard, or some random USB gadget, gets blocked. On particularly sensitive hosts, like domain controllers, jump boxes, kiosks, you can go even further: disable data capable ports in firmware or through the registry / group policy, add physical port blockers if you can, and prevent installation of new device classes so that only essential HID devices work at all.User Behavior and Physical Security HygieneFinally user behavior and physical security, are what turn these mitigations into a real defense instead of just paperwork you know, train the staff never to plug in “found” or unverified USB devices and then make automatic screen locking work, plus the Win+L muscle memory, every time they step away from a machine. Endpoint protection and EDR tools should keep an eye out for unusual keyboard like activity, rapid command chains, and suspicious PowerShell or CMD usage, but also security teams have to actually review those device control and script execution logs, not just let them sit there and decay over time. And when people lock their screens dont expose random ports. Also run with non admin roles, because a Flipper Zero becomes more like another physical attack device that really struggles in a well designed environment, instead of being a $50 shortcut to a million dollar breach.

title: Securing the Return Desk
author: Jacob Weingardt
body: Defeating Warranty Fraud, Keeping Your Business Safe from AI and Digital Deception Warranty fraud is moving fast. The old days, where you could spot a photocopy real quick or catch white-out marks, are basically over. Now both small businesses and bigger enterprise orgs deal with a fresh surge of tech-enabled scams. Forged and altered receipts Fraudsters do not always need advanced graphic design know-how now. Businesses should push direct-to-consumer sales via their own websites, or through physical stores . If you do sell on Amazon, it’s usually best to operate as a direct seller only . When you manage the distribution channel, you don’t need to guess whether a receipt is fake , because you can quickly cross reference the order number against your internal sales database . And if the transaction is not in your system, the claim gets denied pretty fast, no big drama.Mandate Video Evidence Static pictures are super easy to tweak with new AI, but actual video is way harder to fake, like exponentially more difficult to do cleanly. Businesses can require claimants to send in a short continuous recording, basically demonstrating the defect in real time. If they make the person show the product from a few angles, capture the serial number on the device in the same shot, and then physically show the failure happening , companies build this huge technical wall that most scam artists just can’t climb.Implement ERP Serial Number Tracking A serial number should act like a secure key, not simply a label that sits on a cardboard box. Companies should use an Enterprise Resource Planning system to manage every single serial number, from the manufacturing floor all the way through the point of sale. When someone starts a warranty claim , the ERP ought to instantly review the serial number’s record. So if some random person lifts a number off eBay, the ERP can raise an alert because the account , purchase location , and purchase date don’t line up with the original authorized buyer. That stops the whole scheme before any replacement gets shipped out, at least in theory.

title: Operation Riptide: FBI Dismantles First VPN Service
author: Jacob Weingardt
body: FBI’s Operation Riptide Dismantles ‘First VPN Service’ in Major Strike Against Ransomware InfrastructureThe Federal Bureau of Investigation working alongside international law enforcement partners such as Europol and Eurojust, has managed to take down “First VPN Service”, which was a key piece of infrastructure used by global cybercriminal networks. This takedown is being described as the first real win of Operation Riptide, a steady 60-day national enforcement effort , focused on knocking apart the tools and the money pathways of transnational cyber threat groups. Operation Riptide itself was set in motion after a 26% single-year increase in cybercrime, and that spike reportedly led to more than $20 billion in losses for American organizations and citizens last year.The unraveling of First VPN Service Running since 2014, First VPN Service was widely promoted across Russian-language dark web forums as a “premium” way to get full online anonymity. Investigators say it wasn’t just some casual privacy product, it was more or less built to serve cybercriminals in a direct way. According to the allegations, the service let malicious operators send traffic through servers located in 27 different countries, including internal or domestic style nodes in California, Florida, and New York. By hiding where they were coming from, hackers used First VPN for broad network surveying and then to carry out intrusions targeting enterprise systems. The FBI says at least 25 ransomware groups including the infamous Avaddon syndicate depended on this setup in order to breach corporate networks. The takedown, which was led by France’s Direction Régionale de la Police Judiciaire with technical assistance from the FBI’s Boston Division and Cyber Headquarters, led to the seizure of servers across multiple regions and the VPN homepage was swapped out for a law enforcement seizure notice.Tactical ImplicationsOperation Riptide basically marks a pretty aggressive strategic move, leaning hard into messing with the service supply chain that threat actors lean on, which then raises their operational expenses, and you know, all that knock on stuff. By pulling apart so called “safe havens” like First VPN, law enforcement kind of throws systemic uncertainty into the broader cybercriminal landscape. After that, the FBI is getting ready to put out a FLASH report covering the Indicators of Compromise, plus the Tactics Techniques, and Procedures tied to the First VPN Service.Hardening Enterprise InfrastructureFor IT pros and system administrators who run corporate networks, the dismantling of First VPN is a blunt reminder about keeping strict internal security hygiene. Sure, the takedown knocks out one particular tool from the attackers’ toolkit, but the deeper enterprise weaknesses they tried to use are still sitting there. As Operation Riptide keeps going for the next 60 days, the cybersecurity community can expect more enforcement actions, more search warrants, and indictments that are meant to dismantle the underlying infrastructure, the bedrock, of modern cybercrime.Authentication Log AuditsThreat actors utilizing anonymization services often trigger anomalous login attempts. Auditing conditional access policies and continuously monitoring cloud identity platforms, such as Microsoft Entra ID, is critical for detecting reconnaissance efforts.Enforcing Strict Authentication ProtocolsRansomware operators frequently exploit compromised credentials. Ensuring multi-factor authentication is strictly enforced across all user accounts and remote access portals can mitigate the risk of intrusion. If corporate devices become stuck in persistent authentication loops, clearing the local device authentication cache and forcing an MFA re-registration ensures device integrity and blocks ghost sessions.Network-Level DefensesAdministrators should ingest the newly released FBI FLASH indicators of compromise into their security appliances. Proactively blocking traffic to and from known malicious IP addresses and domains associated with the defunct VPN service remains an essential step in safeguarding local network perimeters.

FBI’s Operation Riptide Dismantles ‘First VPN Service’ in Major Strike Against Ransomware Infrastructure

The Federal Bureau of Investigation working alongside international law enforcement partners such as Europol and Eurojust, has managed to take down “First VPN Service”, which was a key piece of infrastructure used by global cybercriminal networks. This takedown is being described as the first real win of Operation Riptide, a steady 60-day national enforcement effort , focused on knocking apart the tools and the money pathways of transnational cyber threat groups. Operation Riptide itself was set in motion after a 26% single-year increase in cybercrime, and that spike reportedly led to more than $20 billion in losses for American organizations and citizens last year.

The unraveling of First VPN Service


Running since 2014, First VPN Service was widely promoted across Russian-language dark web forums as a “premium” way to get full online anonymity. Investigators say it wasn’t just some casual privacy product, it was more or less built to serve cybercriminals in a direct way. According to the allegations, the service let malicious operators send traffic through servers located in 27 different countries, including internal or domestic style nodes in California, Florida, and New York. By hiding where they were coming from, hackers used First VPN for broad network surveying and then to carry out intrusions targeting enterprise systems. The FBI says at least 25 ransomware groups including the infamous Avaddon syndicate depended on this setup in order to breach corporate networks.  

The takedown, which was led by France’s Direction Régionale de la Police Judiciaire with technical assistance from the FBI’s Boston Division and Cyber Headquarters, led to the seizure of servers across multiple regions and the VPN homepage was swapped out for a law enforcement seizure notice.

Tactical Implications

Operation Riptide basically marks a pretty aggressive strategic move, leaning hard into messing with the service supply chain that threat actors lean on, which then raises their operational expenses, and you know, all that knock on stuff. By pulling apart so called “safe havens” like First VPN, law enforcement kind of throws systemic uncertainty into the broader cybercriminal landscape. After that, the FBI is getting ready to put out a FLASH report covering the Indicators of Compromise, plus the Tactics Techniques, and Procedures tied to the First VPN Service.

Hardening Enterprise Infrastructure

For IT pros and system administrators who run corporate networks, the dismantling of First VPN is a blunt reminder about keeping strict internal security hygiene. Sure, the takedown knocks out one particular tool from the attackers’ toolkit, but the deeper enterprise weaknesses they tried to use are still sitting there. As Operation Riptide keeps going for the next 60 days, the cybersecurity community can expect more enforcement actions, more search warrants, and indictments that are meant to dismantle the underlying infrastructure, the bedrock, of modern cybercrime.

Authentication Log Audits

Threat actors utilizing anonymization services often trigger anomalous login attempts. Auditing conditional access policies and continuously monitoring cloud identity platforms, such as Microsoft Entra ID, is critical for detecting reconnaissance efforts.

Enforcing Strict Authentication Protocols

Ransomware operators frequently exploit compromised credentials. Ensuring multi-factor authentication is strictly enforced across all user accounts and remote access portals can mitigate the risk of intrusion. If corporate devices become stuck in persistent authentication loops, clearing the local device authentication cache and forcing an MFA re-registration ensures device integrity and blocks ghost sessions.

Network-Level Defenses


Administrators should ingest the newly released FBI FLASH indicators of compromise into their security appliances. Proactively blocking traffic to and from known malicious IP addresses and domains associated with the defunct VPN service remains an essential step in safeguarding local network perimeters.

title: WPA2 Password Risk
author: Samuel Abad
body: Your older devices are a gateway into your networkWi-Fi feels invisible. You set it up once, forget about it, and everything just works. Your phone, your laptop, your thermostat, your gaming console all connected to the same network. But that convenience comes with a tradeoff most people never think about, and it starts with the devices you trust the most.We tested two routers, one you can pick up at any Walmart or Target, and a business-class model commonly found in small offices across the US. Using a Nintendo Switch OLED and an Android tablet, we were able to recover the Wi-Fi password on both. Not through some exotic exploit. Not by breaking the router itself. We used the devices against the network they were already connected to. This was a simple attack that is widely detailed online and easy to execute.The lock on your door is only as strong as your weakest keyModern routers support a security standard called WPA3, which makes your Wi-Fi significantly harder to crack. The problem is that older devices, game consoles, smart TVs, thermostats, budget tablets, use chips that only support an older standard called WPA2. These devices cannot use WPA3, no matter how new your router is.To keep those older devices connected, most routers run what is called mixed mode: WPA3 for newer devices, WPA2 for older ones, all on the same network. Your iPhone negotiates the stronger connection. Your Nintendo Switch takes the weaker one. Both end up on your Wi-Fi.That WPA2 connection is the door.When a WPA2 device connects to your network, it performs a brief exchange with your router called a handshake, a small packet of data that proves the device knows your password without sending the password in plain text. An attacker within range of your Wi-Fi can capture that handshake passively, without ever touching your router or any of your devices. Once captured, they take it offline and run it against a list of common passwords until one matches.If your password is common, short, or appeared in any previous data breach, it will fall. If it is strong and unique, the attacker moves on.This works everywhereThe Switch OLED we used was connected to a UDR7, a business-class UniFi router that supports WPA3 and costs significantly more than a consumer device. It did not matter. The moment a WPA2 device joined the network, the attack surface existed. The router's capabilities became irrelevant for that connection.This is not a flaw in any specific router. It is a fundamental characteristic of how WPA2 works, and it applies to every network running mixed mode, which is most home networks in use today.Anyone can do thisThe password in our test was cracked using free tools on a free operating system that anyone can download right now. This was not a movie-style hack. It was not the kind of thing you see on Mr. Robot, where a genius in a dark room types furiously for ten minutes. It was a step-by-step process that anyone with a computer and a search engine can follow. The guides are already out there.That is what makes this worth paying attention to. The threat is not some sophisticated attacker with specialized equipment. It could be a teenager curious about how it works. It could be a neighbor who would rather piggyback off your connection than pay for their own upgrade. The intent does not have to be malicious for the outcome to affect you.So what can you do about it?There are two realistic paths, and neither is perfect.Strengthen your password. This does not close the door, but it makes the door much harder to open. A long, random password that has never appeared in a data breach forces an attacker to abandon the wordlist approach and move to more resource-intensive methods, enough friction that most will simply move on. You can check whether your current password has been exposed at haveibeenpwned.com/Passwords and test its strength at bitwarden.com/password-strength. This option keeps all your devices connected and costs nothing.Switch to WPA3 only. This closes the door entirely for WPA2 attacks. The tradeoff is real: any device that does not support WPA3 will lose Wi-Fi access completely. That includes most Amazon and Google smart home devices, older game consoles, budget security cameras, smart plugs, and many printers. Depending on how your home is set up, this could mean several devices going offline until replaced or moved to a separate network.Some routers allow you to create a secondary SSID, a second Wi-Fi network, running WPA2 specifically for legacy devices, isolated from your main network. This is a reasonable middle ground, but it requires a router that supports it and some comfort with network configuration.There is no option that gives you full compatibility and full security at the same time. That is the honest answer.The bigger pictureThe devices sitting quietly in your living room, the thermostat, the vacuum, the old gaming console, were not designed with your network security in mind. They were designed to be easy to use. The responsibility for what they expose on your network falls on you by default, and most people do not know it exists.Knowing it exists is the first step.
bodyHtml:
Your older devices are a gateway into your network


Wi-Fi feels invisible. You set it up once, forget about it, and everything just works. Your phone, your laptop, your thermostat, your gaming console all connected to the same network. But that convenience comes with a tradeoff most people never think about, and it starts with the devices you trust the most.

We tested two routers, one you can pick up at any Walmart or Target, and a business-class model commonly found in small offices across the US. Using a Nintendo Switch OLED and an Android tablet, we were able to recover the Wi-Fi password on both. Not through some exotic exploit. Not by breaking the router itself. We used the devices against the network they were already connected to. This was a simple attack that is widely detailed online and easy to execute.

The lock on your door is only as strong as your weakest key


Modern routers support a security standard called WPA3, which makes your Wi-Fi significantly harder to crack. The problem is that older devices, game consoles, smart TVs, thermostats, budget tablets, use chips that only support an older standard called WPA2. These devices cannot use WPA3, no matter how new your router is.

To keep those older devices connected, most routers run what is called mixed mode: WPA3 for newer devices, WPA2 for older ones, all on the same network. Your iPhone negotiates the stronger connection. Your Nintendo Switch takes the weaker one. Both end up on your Wi-Fi.

That WPA2 connection is the door.

When a WPA2 device connects to your network, it performs a brief exchange with your router called a handshake, a small packet of data that proves the device knows your password without sending the password in plain text. An attacker within range of your Wi-Fi can capture that handshake passively, without ever touching your router or any of your devices. Once captured, they take it offline and run it against a list of common passwords until one matches.



This works everywhere

The Switch OLED we used was connected to a UDR7, a business-class UniFi router that supports WPA3 and costs significantly more than a consumer device. It did not matter. The moment a WPA2 device joined the network, the attack surface existed. The router's capabilities became irrelevant for that connection.

This is not a flaw in any specific router. It is a fundamental characteristic of how WPA2 works, and it applies to every network running mixed mode, which is most home networks in use today.


Anyone can do this


The password in our test was cracked using free tools on a free operating system that anyone can download right now. This was not a movie-style hack. It was not the kind of thing you see on Mr. Robot, where a genius in a dark room types furiously for ten minutes. It was a step-by-step process that anyone with a computer and a search engine can follow. The guides are already out there.

That is what makes this worth paying attention to. The threat is not some sophisticated attacker with specialized equipment. It could be a teenager curious about how it works. It could be a neighbor who would rather piggyback off your connection than pay for their own upgrade. The intent does not have to be malicious for the outcome to affect you.


So what can you do about it?


There are two realistic paths, and neither is perfect.

Strengthen your password. This does not close the door, but it makes the door much harder to open. A long, random password that has never appeared in a data breach forces an attacker to abandon the wordlist approach and move to more resource-intensive methods, enough friction that most will simply move on. You can check whether your current password has been exposed at haveibeenpwned.com/Passwords and test its strength at bitwarden.com/password-strength. This option keeps all your devices connected and costs nothing.

Switch to WPA3 only. This closes the door entirely for WPA2 attacks. The tradeoff is real: any device that does not support WPA3 will lose Wi-Fi access completely. That includes most Amazon and Google smart home devices, older game consoles, budget security cameras, smart plugs, and many printers. Depending on how your home is set up, this could mean several devices going offline until replaced or moved to a separate network.

Some routers allow you to create a secondary SSID, a second Wi-Fi network, running WPA2 specifically for legacy devices, isolated from your main network. This is a reasonable middle ground, but it requires a router that supports it and some comfort with network configuration.

There is no option that gives you full compatibility and full security at the same time. That is the honest answer.


The bigger picture


The devices sitting quietly in your living room, the thermostat, the vacuum, the old gaming console, were not designed with your network security in mind. They were designed to be easy to use. The responsibility for what they expose on your network falls on you by default, and most people do not know it exists.

Knowing it exists is the first step.

title: Cybercrime's Record Surge
author: Jacob Weingardt
body: A Quarter-Century of Catching Cyber-Crooks: FBI Report Reveals a Record-Breaking 20 Billion Dollars in Digital Heists A Milestone in Cybercrime Tracking. In 2025, the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) marked its 25th anniversary as the central hub for reporting cyber-enabled crime. Over the past quarter-century, reporting has skyrocketed from a few thousand complaints a month to an average of nearly 3,000 complaints every single day. The year 2025 set a staggering new record, with the IC3 receiving over 1 million complaints that amounted to a massive 20.877 billion dollars in total losses. This represents a 26% increase in financial losses compared to the previous year, highlighting the escalating and costly nature of the modern cyber threat landscape.The Financial Toll of Investment and AI Scams.Investment-related fraud proved to be the most financially devastating cybercrime, draining over 8.6 billion dollars from victims in 2025. Much of this devastation is driven by cryptocurrency investment scams, which alone accounted for 7.2 billion dollars in losses as sophisticated criminal enterprises manipulated victims into fraudulent platforms. Furthermore, the integration of artificial intelligence into cybercrime is a growing concern, making synthetic content and personalized scams increasingly difficult to detect. In 2025, the IC3 received over 22,000 complaints referencing the use of AI, resulting in adjusted losses exceeding 893 million dollars. Targeting the Most Vulnerable Populations. Cybercriminals continue to aggressively target vulnerable demographics, with elder fraud and crimes against minors showing alarming trends. Individuals over the age of 60 filed more than 201,000 complaints, suffering disproportionate losses of over 7.7 billion dollars. On the other end of the spectrum, there has been a serious rise in cybercrimes targeting minors, particularly driven by sextortion, cyberbullying, and online grooming. The IC3 received over 13,000 complaints from complainants 17 years old or younger, and referred over 5,700 submissions involving minors to the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children. Fighting Back and Recovering Assets.Despite the grim statistics, the FBI continues to actively disrupt cyber-criminal networks and recover stolen funds. The IC3 Recovery Asset Team utilizes the Financial Fraud Kill Chain to assist victims, successfully freezing over 679 million dollars in 2025 with a 58% success rate. Additionally, specialized initiatives like Operation Level Up have identified and notified thousands of cryptocurrency investment fraud victims, preventing an estimated 225.8 million dollars in further losses. Through global collaboration and new task forces like the Scam Center Strike Force, law enforcement is actively dismantling the infrastructure that weaponizes the internet against citizens
